summary: Documents how BGP-4 satisfied the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard, summarizing its key features and analyzing scaling and performance. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1774 is a review of BGP, the protocol routers use to exchange reachability information with other networks. It explains how BGP works and then works out how much bandwidth, processor time and memory it needs as the Internet grows.

questions: how much bandwidth does bgp use
subtitle: A report showing BGP-4 meets the bar for Draft Standard, with a look at its bandwidth, memory and scaling.

tldr.problem: A routing protocol must show that it works well and scales before it can advance to Draft Standard, and the Internet was growing fast.
tldr.mechanism: The report summarises BGP-4's key features, path attributes, the AS-PATH, incremental updates and aggregation, and then estimates the bandwidth, CPU and memory each of them costs.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that BGP should have no scaling problems in link bandwidth or CPU while the Internet stays stable, and that the memory limit comes mainly from the flat addressing of IP rather than from BGP itself.

facts.label: Extra memory for AS paths
facts.value: Less than 7 percent of total memory

today: RFC 1774 is an Informational report, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It analyses BGP-4 as specified in RFC 1771 and reflects the Internet of March 1995.

sections.title: Purpose of the Report
sections.content:
The purpose of the report is to document how the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard have been satisfied by the Border Gateway Protocol version 4, BGP-4. It summarises the key features of BGP and analyses the protocol with respect to scaling and performance. The report calls itself the first of two reports on the BGP protocol.

BGP-4 is an inter-autonomous system routing protocol designed for TCP/IP internets. An autonomous system, in this report's terms, is a network with its own internal routing scheme. Version 1 of BGP was published in RFC 1105, version 2 in RFC 1163 and version 3 in RFC 1267. The changes between versions are explained in Appendix 2 of the protocol specification, RFC 1771, and possible applications of BGP in the Internet are documented in RFC 1772.

The report is by P. Traina of cisco Systems and was published in March 1995. It is one of a series of documents produced by the IDR/BGP Working Group of the IETF, and it follows an earlier version of the same text, with RFC 1265 provided by Yakov Rekhter.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a method is promoted to a more official level, someone has to show that it really works. This report is that evidence for BGP.

sections.title: Key Features of BGP-4
sections.content:
BGP is an inter-autonomous system routing protocol, used between multiple autonomous systems. It assumes that routing inside an autonomous system is done by an intra-autonomous system protocol, and makes no assumptions about which one, so the autonomous systems need not all run the same interior protocol. It imposes no constraints on the underlying Internet topology, and the information it exchanges is enough to construct a graph of autonomous system connectivity, from which routing loops may be pruned and some routing policy decisions may be enforced.

The key features are the notion of path attributes and aggregation of network layer reachability information. Path attributes give BGP flexibility and expandability. They are partitioned into well-known and optional, and the provision for optional attributes allows experimentation that may involve a group of BGP routers without affecting the rest of the Internet. The report compares this to the way new options are added to the Telnet protocol.

The most important path attribute is the AS-PATH. Reachability information traversing the Internet is augmented by the list of autonomous systems it has passed through, and that list allows straightforward suppression of routing loops. It also serves as a powerful mechanism for policy-based routing. BGP-4 extends AS-PATH to include sets of autonomous systems as well as lists, so a generated aggregate route can carry path information from the more specific routes used to generate it.

The algorithm fits neither a pure distance vector nor a pure link state. Carrying a complete AS path allows a router to reconstruct large portions of the overall topology, which is like link state, while exchanging only the routes currently in use between peers is like distance vector. To conserve bandwidth and processing power, BGP uses incremental updates: after the initial exchange of complete routing information, a pair of routers exchanges only the changes. That technique requires a reliable transport, so BGP uses TCP. BGP-4 also added route aggregation, so that information about groups of networks can be represented as a single entity. The protocol is self-contained, specifying how routing information is exchanged both between BGP speakers in different autonomous systems and between speakers within a single one, and it supports carrying exterior routes derived from EGP or OSPF as well as statically defined ones, for graceful coexistence.
sections.plainLanguage: Each route carries a list of the networks it passed through, so a message can never go round in circles. After the first large exchange, neighbours only share what changed.

sections.title: Link Bandwidth and CPU Cost
sections.content:
Immediately after the initial BGP connection setup, the peers exchange a complete set of routing information. If N is the total number of routes in the Internet, M the mean AS distance, and A the total number of autonomous systems, and the networks are assumed to be uniformly distributed among the autonomous systems, then the worst case bandwidth consumed during the initial exchange between a pair of BGP speakers is MR = O(N + M * A). The report's table gives typical figures, and marks the row for 20,000 NLRI with a mean AS distance of 8 and 400 autonomous systems, at 86,000 bytes, as the actual size of the Internet when the document was published.

Most of that bandwidth goes on the exchange of the reachability information itself. BGP-4 was created specifically to reduce the number of such entries carried by border routers. Together with CIDR, BGP-4 introduced the supernet, a power-of-two aggregation of more than one class-based network. Because a few large aggregate blocks are advertised instead of many small class-based networks, and because space is reserved for future expansion, the report says it is difficult to estimate the actual reduction BGP-4 brought. The better measure is to sample the number of entries in the globally connected Internet and compare it with the growth rate projected before BGP-4 was deployed. In January 1994 a router carrying a full routing load had approximately 19,000 network entries, and the growth rate was estimated at over 1000 new networks per month and increasing. After widespread deployment of BGP-4 the growth rate dropped significantly, and a sample at the end of November 1994 showed approximately 21,000 entries, as opposed to the expected 30,000.

CPU cycles consumed by BGP depend only on the stability of the Internet. If the Internet is stable, the only bandwidth and CPU consumed are the KEEPALIVE messages, which are exchanged only between peers, at a suggested frequency of 30 seconds, are 19 octets long and require virtually no processing, giving about 5 bits per second of bandwidth. If the Internet is unstable, only the changes travel, in UPDATE messages, and the worst case bandwidth is O(C * M) for C changes per second. In practice routing changes show strong locality with respect to the AS path, so routes that change are likely to have a common AS path and several networks can be grouped into one UPDATE message.

Since in the steady state the cost depends only on stability and is completely independent of the number of networks, the report concludes that BGP should have no scaling problems in link bandwidth and CPU as the Internet grows, provided the stability of inter-AS connectivity can be controlled. That could be addressed with some form of dampening, such as hold downs, which given the nature of BGP should be a local matter for each autonomous system. The report stresses that BGP by itself does not introduce instabilities, and that observations in the NSFNET show the instabilities are largely due to ill-behaved routing within the autonomous systems, so the right fix is stable interior routing schemes. Comparing the two protocols, EGP exchanges complete information periodically, usually every 3 minutes, so even BGP's extreme worst case equals EGP's steady state.
sections.plainLanguage: When things are calm, BGP only sends a short 'still here' note every so often. It shares news only when something changes, which costs far less than repeating everything over and over.

sections.title: Memory Requirements and Scaling Limits
sections.content:
Worst-case memory for BGP is MR = O((N + M * A) * K), where K is the number of BGP speakers a system peers with. In the current NSFNET Backbone, with N = 2110, A = 59 and M = 5, and each network stored as 4 octets and each autonomous system as 2 octets, the overhead of storing the AS path information on top of the exterior routes is less than 7 percent of total memory usage. Before BGP was introduced in the NSFNET Backbone, memory on routers running EGP was on the order of O(N * K), so the extra overhead after BGP was less than 7 percent there too.

Because the mean AS distance grows very slowly, the worst case memory requirement is in practice the total number of networks in the Internet times the number of peers the local system peers with. The report expects the number of networks to grow much faster than the average number of peers per router, so memory scaling is dominated by the number of networks. The report's table runs from 27,000 for 2,100 networks up to 1,040,000 for 100,000 networks, with the peer counts and mean distances assumed in each row.

The report then puts BGP's memory needs in perspective by looking at forwarding tables alone. The forwarding tables in the NSFNET Backbone routers carry well over 20,000 entries, and the question of whether a router with 200,000 entries is possible is completely independent of BGP. It quotes Paul Tsuchiya's review of BGP in March 1990: BGP does not scale well, and this is not really the fault of BGP but of the flat IP address space, because given a flat address space any routing protocol must carry network numbers in its updates. With CIDR and BGP-4 the report says an attempt has been made to reduce this limitation, but history cannot be erased and BGP-4 cannot solve the problems inherent in inefficient assignment of future address blocks. It repeats that BGP's limits with respect to memory are directly related to the addressing scheme of IP, and that BGP would scale much better with more flexible addressing. It adds that BGP was extended with only minor additions to support hierarchies of autonomous systems, and that such hierarchies, combined with an addressing scheme allowing more flexible aggregation, could give practically unlimited scaling to BGP-like protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Remembering every address takes space, and that is mostly because of how addresses were handed out in the past, not because of BGP. Grouping addresses together helps, and grouping the networks themselves would help more.

sections.title: Where BGP Applies
sections.content:
The report quotes the rule that decides which policies BGP can enforce: an autonomous system advertises to its neighbour autonomous systems only those routes that it itself uses. That rule reflects the hop-by-hop routing paradigm used throughout the current Internet. Some policies cannot be supported by that paradigm and would need techniques such as source routing. For example, BGP does not let one autonomous system send traffic to a neighbour intending that the traffic take a different route from the traffic originating in the neighbour itself. On the other hand, BGP can support any policy that conforms to the hop-by-hop paradigm, and since the current Internet uses only that paradigm, the report calls BGP highly applicable as an inter-AS routing protocol for the current Internet.

It adds that BGP is almost a necessity as well. Operational experience with EGP showed it to be highly inadequate: the topological restrictions it imposes are unjustifiable from the technical point of view and unenforceable from the practical one, and its inability to handle information exchange between peers efficiently is a cause of severe routing instabilities in the operational Internet. By contrast, the information provided by BGP suits a variety of routing policies.

Rather than predicting the future and loading BGP with functions that may not be needed, the designers took a different approach: the protocol contains only the essential functionality, while providing flexible mechanisms within itself that allow its functionality to expand. The report argues that this design should let BGP address new or evolving requirements with relative ease, and points to the way new features, such as repairing a partitioned autonomous system, are already being introduced in the protocol. In summary, BGP is well suited to the current Internet, which uses IP as its Internet Protocol and the hop-by-hop paradigm, and it is hard to speculate whether it would suit environments where other protocols are used for internetting or where the routing paradigm is different.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP works well for passing traffic along one hop at a time, which is how the Internet worked then. It cannot do things that need a whole route chosen in advance.
